items.text: Clients usually come to a studio with a specific request. A rebrand. A website redesign. A packaging refresh. Those requests are almost never wrong, but they are almost never the whole problem either.

A rebrand often means the positioning drifted before the visual identity did. A website redesign often means the naming stopped working before the site did. A packaging refresh often signals a distrib

style.fontFamily: "Mona Sans Variable", "Mona Sans Variable Placeholder", sans-serif

items.text: The first thirty minutes of a discovery call are the most valuable minutes in the whole engagement. We are listening for what the client is not saying as much as what they are. Where do they stumble i
Those tells tell us what the brief actually needs to solve, which is often not what the client wrote in their intro email.

style.fontFamily: "Mona Sans Variable", "Mona Sans Variable Placeholder", sans-serif

items.text: By the end of the call, we usually reframe the project. Not to talk the client into a bigger engagement. To make sure the engagement we agree on is aimed at the right problem. Sometimes that means we

style.fontFamily: "Mona Sans Variable", "Mona Sans Variable Placeholder", sans-serif

items.text: Why this is not scope creep
Scope creep happens when the definition of the project changes after work has started. What we are describing is the opposite: doing the definition properly before work starts, so no one is surprised
The brief that comes in the email is a symptom. The brief we agree on the call is the actual project. That is the whole difference.
